items.title: Why re-running a failed migration only finishes the rest
items.body:
The engine compares the desired flat state with the actual state each time it runs. After a partial failure, the parts that succeeded already match, so the next diff contains only what is still missing, and applying it converges. ADR-004 names this retry-is-repair and calls convergence a design property rather than an ops runbook.

- *Roll back, then replay*: there is no transactional rollback across DDL and metadata.
- *Operator must mark it repaired*: retrying is the repair.
- *Reapply everything with IF NOT EXISTS*: the diff avoids redoing completed actions.

excerpts.quote: after partial failure, re-running computes only the

items.title: Why a shared workspaceId column cannot work here
items.body:
A discriminator column assumes all tenants share one table shape. Under ADR-002 they do not: one workspace's company table may have columns another's lacks. So a single shared company table cannot exist unless custom data falls back to JSONB or EAV, which ADR-002 already rejected. ADR-003 calls the option incompatible with ADR-002 for that reason.

- *Indexing partitioned tables*: not the reason given.
- *Row-level security unavailable*: RLS is rejected separately, with the same shape objection plus policy cost.
- *Leaking ids through GraphQL*: not mentioned.

excerpts.quote: tenants have different columns, so a shared `company` table cannot exist

items.title: Start here: Twenty, a CRM whose data model is data
items.body:
Twenty is an open-source CRM. This checkout keeps the monorepo under `twenty/`; the server is `packages/twenty-server` (NestJS, TypeORM, Postgres) and the main code for this quest is under `packages/twenty-server/src/engine/`. Beside the code sit several generations of study docs. This quest uses the third and fourth:

1. `fabledocs3/adr-002-metadata-driven-data-model.md`, the foundational decision.
2. `fabledocs3/adr-003-schema-per-workspace-tenancy.md`, how tenants are separated.
3. `fabledocs3/adr-004-flat-entity-migration-engine.md`, how metadata changes reach the database.
4. `fabledocs4/04-sql-tenancy-lab.md`, which makes ADR-003 concrete in `psql`.
5. `fabledocs4/02-capstone-reliable-webhooks.md`, a design project built on these ideas.

Read each ADR as context, decision, alternatives, consequences, evidence, and open at least one evidence path per ADR. The lab says it plainly: the database is the answer key. Where the lab or an ADR names a file, open it and compare.

excerpts.quote: the database is the answer key. Verify everything.

readMore.why: The ADR index and reading order.
How the drills, labs and capstone in fabledocs4 fit together.

items.title: Why workspace schemas are named workspace_ plus base 36
items.body:
`getWorkspaceSchemaName` is a single expression: the prefix `workspace_` followed by `uuidToBase36(workspaceId)`. Re-encoding the 128-bit UUID in base 36 gives a shorter string of lowercase letters and digits, which is a valid Postgres identifier without quoting. So the suffix is the workspace id itself, just written differently.

- *UUID without hyphens*: the hex form is converted, not just stripped.
- *ws_ plus eight hex digits*: the full id is encoded, and the prefix is `workspace_`.
- *The subdomain*: subdomains can change; the schema name comes from the immutable id.

items.title: Why position is not a base entity field
items.body:
`BaseWorkspaceEntity` is a four-line abstract class: `id`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt` and `deletedAt: string | null`. The lab's parenthesis lists 'position' among the columns every workspace table gets, but the base class does not declare it. Any `position` column on a table comes from that object's own definition. The lab tells you to confirm rather than assume, so the code is keyed.

- *Five fields including position*: position is not in the class.
- *id and position only*: the timestamps and deletedAt are declared right there.
- *deletedAt per object*: it is in the base class, which is what makes soft delete uniform.

excerpts.quote: export abstract class BaseWorkspaceEntity { id: string; createdAt: string; updatedAt: string; deletedAt: string | null;

items.title: Why a rolled-back mutation leaves no outbox row
items.body:
Writing the outbox row in the same transaction as the record change makes the two atomic: they commit together or not at all. Milestone 1's first acceptance test checks the 'not at all' side: a mutation whose transaction rolls back must leave no outbox row, so no webhook is ever sent for a change that did not happen. The second test checks the other side: after commit, a crash before dispatch loses nothing.

- *A cancelled row*: rollback removes the row with everything else.
- *Dispatched as a draft*: there is nothing to dispatch.
- *Deleted by a cron later*: no cleanup is needed when the row never commits.

excerpts.quote: a mutation whose transaction rolls back leaves *no* outbox row

items.title: Why the capstone aims for at-least-once
items.body:
Delivering a webhook means a database row and an HTTP request to someone else's server. No transaction can cover both, so a crash can always fall between sending and recording. The capstone therefore promises at-least-once delivery and gives consumers what they need to deduplicate, and it says exactly-once is not on the menu.

- *Exactly-once with a transaction*: the POST cannot be part of a database transaction.
- *At-most-once with logging*: that is the current behaviour being fixed.
- *Best-effort with daily replay*: not the stated target.

items.title: Why diffing beats replaying a change log
items.body:
Replay assumes the database's real state is exactly what the log says it should be. With runtime DDL against a live database, steps fail and people intervene by hand, so that assumption breaks and replay produces what the ADR calls confident wrongness. Diffing the desired state against the actual state starts from what is really there, so it self-heals.

- *Too slow*: speed is not the reason given.
- *A second database*: storage is not mentioned.
- *Transactional DDL*: the ADR does say DDL and metadata writes cannot be coupled transactionally, but that argues against two-phase commit, not against replay.

excerpts.quote: replay then produces confident wrongness, whereas diffing against *actual* state self-heals

items.title: Concept: diff-driven migrations and the transactional outbox
items.body:
A metadata change such as 'add a field' must update metadata rows, run real DDL, and refresh caches, and these cannot always share one transaction. ADR-004's answer is borrowed from tools like Terraform: describe the **desired state**, diff it against the **actual state**, and apply only the difference. While reading, ask what happens when an apply stops halfway and is started again, and compare that with the alternatives the ADR rejected.

The capstone applies a related idea to webhooks. A **transactional outbox** writes a record of 'this event must be delivered' in the same database transaction as the change that caused it; a separate **relay** later reads unsent rows, sends them and marks them sent. Read milestone 0's seven design questions first, then the acceptance criteria of each milestone. For every crash point you can think of (before commit, after commit, after the HTTP POST, after marking), write down what the consumer would see, and which design decision handles it. Finally, read the stated target semantics and the sentence about exactly-once.

excerpts.quote: Metadata changes are **declarative and diff-driven**, Terraform-style.

readMore.why: Milestone 0: the design doc and its review gate.

items.title: Concept: metadata-driven objects and one schema per workspace
items.body:
Most applications fix their tables at compile time. Twenty lets every customer define objects and fields at runtime, so the server must learn the shape of the data from **metadata rows** on each request. Three ideas follow from that, and the ADRs explain each.

- **Same rails.** Ask how the built-in objects (company, person) relate to a customer's custom objects. Open `src/engine/twenty-orm/base.workspace-entity.ts` and the `src/modules/company/` folder, and list exactly which fields the base class declares.
- **Rejected alternatives.** ADR-002 rejects three designs. For each, write one sentence on what goes wrong; the reasons differ.
- **Caching.** The metadata a request needs is cached per workspace. Think about what a stale copy would break.

For tenancy, ADR-003 compares four layouts (schema per workspace, discriminator column, database per tenant, row-level security). Note why each loser lost, then open `src/engine/workspace-datasource/utils/get-workspace-schema-name.util.ts` and work out what a workspace schema is called. The lab's Part 4 asks what a bug would have to do to leak data across tenants: answer it before reading ADR-003's consequences.

excerpts.quote: Object and field definitions are **rows, not code**.

readMore.why: How a workspace id becomes a Postgres schema name.

items.title: Why a stale metadata cache is a correctness bug
items.body:
Every request is served from a per-workspace projection of the metadata (`src/engine/workspace-cache/`), and the GraphQL schema, ORM mappings and permissions are resolved from it. If that projection is out of date, the API can expose or reject the wrong fields, so ADR-002 says staleness becomes an API-correctness bug, not a performance bug.

- *Performance only*: the ADR rejects exactly that framing.
- *Settings UI only*: the cache feeds the serving path of every request.
- *Nothing visible*: requests read the cached projection rather than the metadata tables each time.

excerpts.quote: cache staleness becomes an API-correctness bug, not a performance bug

items.title: Why EAV tables were rejected
items.body:
EAV stores each value as a row of (entity, attribute, value). ADR-002 rejects it because query complexity explodes into multi-way self-joins, indexes become useless, and the team would end up reimplementing a query planner in application code. Real tables and columns per workspace avoid all three.

- *A row cap*: the ADR mentions no limit on rows.
- *Cannot store relations*: the objection is cost and complexity, not impossibility.
- *Redeploy per field*: that is the objection to the code-generation alternative.

excerpts.quote: query complexity explodes (multi-way self-joins), indexes are useless

items.title: Why a cross-tenant leak needs a constructed schema name
items.body:
Each workspace's records live in its own Postgres schema. A query physically targets one schema, so there is no shared table where a forgotten predicate returns other tenants' rows. To leak data, code would have to build and use another workspace's schema name. That is why ADR-003 calls isolation structural, and why the lab points you at the places where schema names are constructed.

- *A missing WHERE workspaceId*: there is no shared table to filter.
- *A stale search_path*: not the mechanism the ADR or lab describe; queries target an explicit schema.
- *A foreign record id*: the id is simply not in the caller's schema.

excerpts.quote: cross-tenant leakage requires constructing a wrong schema name, not just forgetting a WHERE clause

items.title: Why a relay crash after the POST yields a duplicate
items.body:
The relay sends first and marks second. If it dies between the two, the row is still unmarked, so the next relay tick claims it and sends it again. The consumer receives the same event twice. The capstone's review gate makes this the test of your design: the right answer is 'a duplicate, which is why the idempotency key exists'.

- *The lock rolls back the POST*: an HTTP request that was sent cannot be undone by a database rollback.
- *A single delivery*: the mark is what records 'sent', and it never happened.
- *An error response*: consumers do not know about the outbox's marking.

excerpts.quote: a duplicate, which is why the idempotency key exists

items.title: Why standard objects ride the same rails as custom ones
items.body:
ADR-002's decision says the standard objects in `src/modules/` (company, person, opportunity) are workspace entities extending `base.workspace-entity.ts` and are seeded into metadata like any custom object. Because both kinds go through the same metadata, ORM, GraphQL and permission machinery, a feature cannot work for built-in objects and fail for custom ones.

- *Fixed TypeORM tables in core*: that is how platform data (users, workspaces, billing) is stored, not CRM objects.
- *JSONB documents*: the ADR rejects a JSONB custom-fields design.
- *Code-generated per tenant*: also a rejected alternative.

excerpts.quote: standard and custom ride identical rails
